title: Egypt's Mummified Cats Lived Hard Lives, Skulls Show
paragraphs: The cats of ancient Egypt have long been romanticised as pampered, sacred companions, and the sheer volume of feline mummies appears to bear that out. A study of their skulls suggests that, for many of the animals, the reality was considerably grimmer.

Wim Van Neer, Bea De Cupere and colleagues at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences examined 131 mummified skulls from Beni Hassan and reported their findings in the Journal of Archaeological Science. Fourteen bore injuries, and nineteen showed tiny perforations in the eye sockets that are consistent with infection or nutritional stress. Around 86 percent of the animals were adults, against some 20 percent in earlier surveys of cat mummies. Certain lesions looked to have been inflicted by a sharp metal implement and, being unhealed, probably killed the animal. "This is not what one would expect for animals destined to become votive mummies," De Cupere remarked.

The authors blame overcrowding, which would inevitably have bred stress, aggression and contagion. Even so, they stop short of an indictment. A skull-only sample makes diagnosis tentative, and the violence cuts both ways: a fatal blow may have been the opening act of mummification, while healed fractures show that others endured and recovered. To brand the ancient breeders cruel on this evidence would be to read more into bone than bone can say.

questions.q: What does the 86 percent adult figure suggest?
questions.a: The animals were not typical young cats in earlier samples, which is unexpected for votive mummies.

questions.q: Why do the authors stop short of condemning the ancient breeders?
questions.a: Because the sample was only skulls, and the violence could be fatal blows before mummification or survivable injuries.

questions.q: Which evidence suggests some cats died from violence?
questions.a: Unhealed lesions that appear to come from a sharp metal implement.
